extracted.intended_audience: experimental natural philosophers / Royal Society contributors and readers (practicing scientists reporting experiments)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing detailed experimental reports and observations for publication in a learned society journal: describe apparatus, materials, procedures, measurements, repetitions, controls, and argumentation so others can judge and reproduce results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat trials and independent witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Report repetitions and independent confirmations: 'I not only made trial in my own hand, when in different tempers as to heat and cold, but the hands of others, who were not a little surprised and pleased at the event... by which means I had, and still have, divers witnesses of the truth of the experiment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform experiments multiple times and, where possible, have others repeat them or witness the effect; record that witnesses tried the procedure (who, how often) to strengthen credibility and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide materials preparation protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Give explicit preparation methods for reagents and materials (e.g., calx of gold by quartation or by making an amalgama and dissolving the mercury in aquafortis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document how key materials were prepared, including alternative workable recipes and practical notes (e.g., washing, drying, heating) so others can reproduce the same material states that affect outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and address alternative explanations (controls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate sceptical scruples and perform control experiments to rule out confounders: e.g., to exclude skin-contact heating the author kept the mixture in a paper and tried leaves of gold to test whether acid residues or preparation methods caused the heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and report control experiments (different substrates, mock treatments) that directly test plausible alternative causes; explain how the control results remove the objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report quantities, scale and experimental limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Give amounts and discuss scale effects: 'I made these trials but with a drachm at a time, which scarcely amounts... whereas, if I could have made the experiment with a spoonful or two ... the heat would have been intense enough...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State precise masses/volumes used, and discuss how scale (small vs large samples) may affect results or risks; note when resource limits restrict ideal protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use instruments and quantify measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ measuring apparatus and report quantitative observations (e.g., using a gauge so that 'the quicksilver rose about an inch in the gauge', or measuring mercury rise to infer gas volumes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible use calibrated instruments, record their readings, and convert instrument data into physically meaningful quantities with units so conclusions can be checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report negative and unsuccessful results
rubrics_metrics.description: Include failed attempts and null results: 'I tried... refined silver... but I could not perceive any heat at all' and leaving lungs between plates 'without success'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document negative trials and unsuccessful alternative methods; these observations help delimit the effect and inform others what not to try or what conditions fail to produce results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe apparatus geometry and experimental conditions precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify the spatial arrangement and conditions of the setup (e.g., prism placement relative to the hole, receiver filling fraction, whether experiments were 'made in clear days', distances that matter, and distinction between schematic demonstration and actual experiment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear descriptions (and where helpful, diagrams) of geometry, distances, orientation, environmental conditions (light, temperature, vacuum degree), and explicitly state when a scheme is demonstrative rather than a literal experimental layout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide time-course and procedural sequence details
rubrics_metrics.description: Report timings and sequences (e.g., insects left in vacuum for an hour, two days, eight days and their differing recovery times; water boiling duration in vacuum and post-heat behaviour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record durations for each step, intervals between manipulations, and evolution of observable states over time to allow replication and interpretation of dynamic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make quantitative inferences with clear assumptions and state uncertainties
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform calculations from data and state assumptions/uncertainties: e.g., deducing 'a fifth part of air in gunpowder' from mercury rise and noting the calculation is 'more uncertain than the former' because of unknowns about packing and volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the arithmetic/derivation linking measurements to inferred quantities, list assumptions explicitly, and comment on confidence and sources of possible error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare substances, conditions and species systematically
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare different materials and biological subjects (e.g., spirit of wine vs water, mercury with gold vs silver, insects vs birds vs mammals) and report differing responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When investigating a phenomenon, test comparable variants (different reagents, species, or states) and tabulate/report contrasts to map scope and generality of the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw hypotheses cautiously and indicate need for further verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate explanatory hypotheses from results but qualify them and point to future tests: 'We should therefore make no difficulty to believe, that all the effect of gunpowder comes from the air which is compressed therein,' yet calculations and uncertainties are discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State conclusions that follow from the data but avoid overstating; explicitly recommend further experiments or lines of evidence to confirm proposed mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground interpretation in existing literature and theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate experimental results to prior work and theory (references to Boyle, Wallis, Newton, and hydrostatics) and advise readers to 'compare with' earlier treatises to resolve controversies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite and compare with prior experiments and theoretical frameworks; show how new data fit or challenge existing doctrines, enabling informed judgment by readers familiar with the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical completeness for professional competence (architecture example)
rubrics_metrics.description: For professional instruction (Blondel on architecture): teach origin/principles and practice of the five orders and required complementary sciences (geometry, arithmetic, mechanics, hydraulics, gnomonics, fortification, perspective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When setting curricula or standards for professional skill, list core subject-matter and allied disciplines necessary to form competent practitioners and justify practical training (e.g., prizes, travel, applied exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish demonstration schemes from experimental reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Make explicit when a displayed scheme is 'the scheme of a demonstration, not of the experiment' (diagrams for proof may differ from the actual experimental setup).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether diagrams are idealized illustrations for argument or faithful reproductions of the performed experiment; provide the latter when reproducibility is intended.
